text: Remind them to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,
to slander no one, to avoid quarreling, to be considerate, showing true gentleness toward all people.

versions.text: to slander no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward everyone.
versions.explanation: πραΰτης means "gentleness/meekness"; "courtesy" loses the moral force of the term, and πᾶσαν means "every/all" rather than "perfect."

versions.text: and to show every kindness and gentleness toward all people.
versions.explanation: Three of the four clauses in the Greek have dropped out: μηδένα βλασφημεῖν ("to slander no one"), ἀμάχους εἶναι ("to avoid quarreling"), and ἐπιεικεῖς ("considerate/forbearing"). Only the final participial clause survives, and the added "kindness and gentleness" doubles up on πραΰτητα. The full list must be restored, and it should continue the infinitive series begun in v.1.

versions.text: to slander no one, to avoid quarreling, to be considerate, showing every kindness toward all people.
versions.explanation: πραΰτης denotes gentleness/meekness, a specific character virtue, rather than the broader "kindness." Since ἐπιεικεῖς is already rendered "considerate," using "gentleness" here keeps the two terms distinct and preserves the moral force of πραΰτης noted in the earlier revision.

text: For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, enslaved to all kinds of passions and pleasures, living in malice and envy, despised and hating one another.
But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for humanity appeared,
he saved us—not because of righteous deeds we had done, but because of his own mercy—through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,
whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,
so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs in the hope of eternal life.

versions.text: so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs with the hope of eternal life.
versions.explanation: κατʼ ἐλπίδα expresses the norm or basis ("in keeping with the hope"), which "in the hope of" conveys better than "with the hope of."

text: This saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have come to believe in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and beneficial for everyone.

versions.text: This saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have come to believe in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for everyone.
versions.explanation: "Profitable" is echoed negatively in v.9 ("unprofitable"); "beneficial" reads more naturally aloud, and καλά is simply "good."

versions.text: These things are good and beneficial for everyone.
versions.explanation: The first three-quarters of the verse is missing: the trustworthy-saying formula (Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος), Paul's charge to Titus (βούλομαί σε διαβεβαιοῦσθαι), and the purpose clause about believers devoting themselves to good works. Without it "These things" has no antecedent and the pivotal instruction to Titus is lost.

text: But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, quarrels, and fights about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless.
After a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a divisive person,

versions.text: Warn a divisive person once, then a second time; after that, have nothing more to do with him,
versions.explanation: The Greek has a single imperative (παραιτοῦ) with the warnings in a prepositional phrase; the current rendering adds an imperative ("Warn") not in the text, though the sense is preserved.

text: knowing that such a person has gone astray and keeps on sinning, self-condemned.

versions.text: knowing that such a person is twisted and sinful; he condemns himself.
versions.explanation: ἁμαρτάνει is a verb ("is sinning"), not an adjective; ἐξέστραπται is perfect passive ("has been turned aside"), and αὐτοκατάκριτος is best rendered as the concluding participial phrase "self-condemned."

text: As soon as I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.
Do everything you can to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, so that they lack nothing.
And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, to meet urgent needs, so that they will not be unfruitful.
Everyone with me sends you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.
